text:
# What's new in Swift: November 2026 Edition | Swift.org
What's new in Swift: November 2026 Edition
Dave Verwer · Dave Lester · November 11, 2026
Welcome to the latest edition of “What’s new in Swift,” a curated digest of releases, news, and discussions from the Swift project and community.
To start things off, our guest contributor shares a timely reminder for anyone relying on CocoaPods:
Hi, I’m Dave Verwer, co-creator of the Swift Package Index and now part of a team at Apple working on a public, cross-platform package registry for Swift. How developers find, share, and manage dependencies across the entire ecosystem is something we think about a lot.
CocoaPods is a dependency manager for Swift and Objective-C Cocoa projects. The project began in 2011, before Swift was publicly available and long before the Swift Package Manager (SwiftPM) existed. For many people who started developing with the iPhone SDK, it was a first look at what a dependency manager could do. Today, Swift has expanded across platforms, and SwiftPM has become the standard for managing dependencies everywhere Swift runs.
Following a two-year sunset period that began in 2024, the CocoaPods project will stop accepting new pods and pod versions on December 2nd, 2026 . With that date less than a month away, I wanted to make sure this milestone is on your radar, and to share what it means for your projects. If your project still uses CocoaPods, this change won’t immediately break your builds. All current pods and versions will still be available, just in a read-only state. However, with pod authors no longer able to publish updates, if you haven’t switched to SwiftPM yet, now is the time.
Most pods in your dependencies that are still being maintained will already be compatible with SwiftPM, and the easiest way to check is to look for them on Swift Package Index . Every package in the index is a SwiftPM package, and if you find any incompatible pods, you can search for an alternative so you don’t leave yourself with unmaintained dependencies.
I’d like to extend a personal thank you to everyone who worked on CocoaPods for creating and maintaining it for the last fifteen years. Their work shaped how the community shares code, and it helped lay the groundwork for the modern, cross-platform package ecosystem Swift has today. I also want to express my admiration for how the team managed this sunset and communicated the transition so clearly.
Now on to other news about Swift:
Videos to watch
- Tim Condon’s ACCU 2026 talk, Incrementally Migrating C++ to a Memory Safe Language with Swift , shows how Swift’s C++ interoperability lets you adopt memory safety incrementally, without rewriting everything at once.
- Building Android App with Swift: First-Hand Experience is a conversation with Pierluigi Cifani, who describes how his team shares business logic and ViewModels between iOS and Android, with native UI on each and Skip bridging the two, in apps like Polymarket.
- Want to build Minecraft mods in Swift? A recent iOSDC Japan lightning talk, Creating a Minecraft Java mod with Swift , shows how, using swift-java to interoperate with Minecraft Java Edition. The speaker’s blog post has the slides and more demo videos. The talk is in Japanese, with an auto-dubbed English track available on YouTube.
Community highlights
- Did you know Optional has a take() method? John Sundell’s Interesting ways of using Swift optionals goes beyond if let , with take() , switching directly on optional enums, and a small isNil(or:) helper that works with key paths.
- What happens when you let the compiler check your whole website? Sindre Sorhus rebuilt his site in Swift , moving off Astro so that broken links and bad metadata become build errors.
- Two server-side frameworks, one team’s experience. Don’t Underestimate Swift shares what engineers at EPAM learned building backends with Hummingbird and Vapor, and how those services compared against FastAPI and Node.js.
- A preview of Embedded Swift support in Swift Testing shows nearly the whole API
[Page continues.]

What’s new in Swift
Dive into the latest features and capabilities.
Swift 6.4
Swift 6.4 delivers improvements designed for developers at every level. A set of ergonomic refinements remove everyday friction, including simplified availability syntax with anyAppleOS and finer-grained control over warnings with the @diagnose attribute. Asynchronous code is now supported in defer statements, guaranteeing cleanup runs whether a function returns or throws. A new iteration protocol extends for-in loops to noncopyable types like Span and InlineArray , letting performance-critical code iterate without unnecessary copying. Foundation sees major performance gains, with URL parsing up to 4x faster. And Swift Testing gains XCTest interoperability for smoother incremental migration.
